statement: In 10 healthy volunteers who received, a month apart and in counterbalanced order, a placebo scan, (S)-ketamine and an equimolar amount of (R)-ketamine, the two mirror-image forms did different things. (S)-ketamine produced a short-lived psychosis-like state: depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances from pseudohallucinations to complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy, with heightened feelings or euphoria reported by 30%, indifference by 30% and heightened anxiety by 40%, alongside higher scores for deactivation, introversion, emotional irritability and anxiety on a mood scale. The same people on (R)-ketamine reported no psychotic symptoms but a state of relaxation, with only trend-level changes on the scales. Every one of the 10 scored higher under (S)- than under (R)-ketamine on both global scales (altered-states score 37.0, SD 12.6, against 15.6, SD 8.6; ego-pathology score 24.6, SD 11.8, against 1.3, SD 1.6). The printed altered-states mean and standard deviation for the (S) condition do not follow from the ten per-person values printed above them, which give 38.2 (SD 10.3); the printed pair is the one printed for racemic ketamine in the companion study, a different ten people (cards sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b). The brain scans went in opposite directions: (S)-ketamine raised glucose metabolism across most regions, while (R)-ketamine tended to lower it, significantly in the temporomedial cortex on both sides (−13.4%) and the left insula (−14%). Blood levels were similar in the two conditions (mean 379 ng/mL, SD 71, against 389, SD 74) (Vollenweider et al., 1997a). Three things limit this. The blind did not hold: every participant recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect, and all had had an (S)-ketamine session beforehand. The two forms were not compared with the racemic mixture in these same people, so the conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic part of racemic ketamine rests on a comparison with the different sample of the companion study, not on anything measured here; the amounts over a session do work out at about the 60% of the racemic amount the paper states, once the shorter infusion is counted (editors' recomputation on card sc_vollenweider_1997a), but the potency ratio behind that choice comes from a pilot study reported in one sentence without a sample size, a method or a reference. And a separate three-person study found no significant difference between the forms in how the body handles them, which with three people and no test statistic says very little (Yanagihara et al., 2003). A 2016 review reports, second-hand, that S-ketamine has about four times the affinity of R-ketamine for the NMDA receptor and has been postulated to be about four times as potent as R-ketamine and twice as potent as the racemate, that R-ketamine slows the elimination of S-ketamine (clearance 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine alone against 18.5 for the S-form inside the racemate in ten healthy men), and that it contradicts itself on which form produces more of the psychosis-like effects: its pharmacodynamics section reports more auditory and visual disturbances with the S-form, while its abstract and summary report fewer such effects with S-ketamine than with the racemate or the R-form. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Ketamine comes in two mirror-image forms, S and R. In one study, 10 healthy people were given each form on different days, a month apart. The S form produced a short psychosis-like state with hallucinations and a changed sense of self; every single person scored higher on it than on the R form. The R form produced no such symptoms, just a relaxed state. Brain scans moved in opposite directions too. But everyone could tell when they had been given a drug, only 10 people took part, and the study did not compare the forms with the ordinary mixture in the same people.
population: 10 healthy volunteers (6 men, 4 women, mean age 30.4 years) screened for absence of personal and family psychiatric history and of non-medical drug use, each acting as their own control; separately, 3 healthy men in the pharmacokinetic study
exposure: Intravenous (S)- or (R)-ketamine (study conditions: a 15 mg induction amount in 20 mL saline over 5 minutes, 5 minutes with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014–0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 minutes, the (R) condition equimolar to the (S) condition)
comparator: The same people's placebo scan and their other enantiomer condition
outcome: Psychopathology and mood ratings for the scan period, and regional brain glucose metabolism during the infusion; in the second study, pharmacokinetic parameters of the two enantiomers
magnitude: Vollenweider et al. (1997a), n=10, within-person: altered-states global score 37.0 (SD 12.6) under (S)-ketamine against 15.6 (SD 8.6) under (R)-ketamine; ego-pathology global score 24.6 (SD 11.8) against 1.3 (SD 1.6); higher under (S) in all 10 participants (editors' calculation of the within-person difference: 22.6 points, SD 6.3, and 23.3 points, SD 10.9; exact two-sided sign test p = 0.002). Emotional reactions under (S): euphoria or heightened feelings 30%, indifference 30%, heightened anxiety 40%. (R)-ketamine: no psychotic symptoms; oceanic boundlessness p<0.06, well-being p<0.09, emotional irritation p<0.08. Glucose metabolism under (R): whole brain −9.8% (p<0.07, not significant), temporomedial cortex −13.4% bilaterally and left insula −14% (p<0.05). Blood levels 269 to 523 ng/mL (mean 379, SD 71) under (S) and 280 to 508 (mean 389, SD 74) under (R).

evidence.extracted: (S)-ketamine produced depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances ranging from pseudohallucinations to elementary and complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy, with auditory changes described as illusions rather than true hallucinations, and emotional reactions of heightened feelings or euphoria in 30%, indifference in 30% and heightened anxiety in 40%; mood-scale scores rose for deactivation (p<0.01), introversion (p<0.05), emotional irritability (p<0.05) and anxiety (p<0.01). Equimolar (R)-ketamine produced no psychotic symptoms in the same people but a state of relaxation, with oceanic boundlessness rising only at trend level (p<0.06), well-being at p<0.09 and emotional irritation falling at p<0.08.

evidence.locator: Table 1, columns S-Ketamine and R-Ketamine (APZ global and EPI global)
evidence.extracted: Per-person global scores: under (S)-ketamine the altered-states scores were 25, 47, 27, 37, 46, 27, 38, 33, 47 and 55 and the ego-pathology scores 10, 25, 25, 39, 24, 17, 27, 10, 21 and 48; under (R)-ketamine they were 10, 16, 9, 11, 15, 10, 8, 15, 29 and 33, and 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 3 and 5. The printed means are 37.0 (SD 12.6) and 24.6 (SD 11.8) against 15.6 (SD 8.6) and 1.3 (SD 1.6). Editors' calculation from those ten pairs: every participant scored higher under (S)-ketamine, the within-person difference being 22.6 points (SD 6.3) for the altered-states score and 23.3 (SD 10.9) for ego pathology (exact two-sided sign test p = 0.002); the printed (S) altered-states mean and SD do not reproduce from the ten values above them, which give 38.2 and 10.3.

evidence.locator: Results › Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: (R)-ketamine tended to lower glucose metabolism across brain regions, in contrast to (S)-ketamine: whole brain −9.8% (p<0.07, not significant), with significant decreases bilaterally in the temporomedial cortex (−13.4%) and in the left insula (−14%), and relative decreases in the right temporal cortex (−4.0%) and bilaterally in the cerebellum (−5.0% and −4.0%, p<0.05).

Blood levels were in the same range in the two conditions: 269 to 523 ng/mL (mean 379, SD 71) under (S)-ketamine and 280 to 508 ng/mL (mean 389, SD 74) under (R)-ketamine, so the difference in effects is not explained by one form reaching a higher level. The paper also states that psychotic symptoms appeared about 5 minutes after the start of the (S)-ketamine infusion at a mean level of 539 ng/mL, which lies above the range printed on the same page and is not reconciled.

The authors report that participants could well tell their (R)-ketamine experience from the placebo measurements, that the ego-pathology scores under (S)-ketamine were about two-thirds of published values in people with first-episode schizophrenia and that two of the five ego dimensions were clearly less affected, and that their conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetically active part of racemic ketamine rests on it having been given at 60% of a racemic amount used in a different sample, not on a racemic condition tested here.

evidence.locator: Materials and method › Phase I: Preliminary drug exposure (2.5) (p. 28); Discussion › Hyperfrontality and psychopathology (4.3), paragraph on (R)-ketamine before the conclusion (p. 36)
evidence.extracted: The paper states that the state of relaxation and elation produced by (R)-ketamine was correctly identified as a drug effect by all of the subjects, and that the weak effects of (R)-ketamine on mood and metabolism have to be read with caution because the sample was small and the mood changes slight. Taken with the preliminary (S)-ketamine session every participant had before the scans, this means the ratings were made in an effectively unblinded condition.

evidence.locator: Results, last (4th) paragraph, which begins on p. 39 and ends at the top of the left column of p. 40
evidence.extracted: In three healthy men, no pharmacokinetic parameter of ketamine or norketamine differed significantly between the (R)- and the (S)-enantiomer, or between the five preparations, by analysis of variance (named in the Methods on p. 39 with 0.05 as the minimal level of significance). No test statistic, degrees of freedom or p-value is printed anywhere in the paper, so this null result in three people cannot be read as evidence that the two forms behave alike in the body.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2 Clinical Pharmacometric Studies of Ketamine in Anesthesia and Pain Therapy, 2nd paragraph (p. 7); Section 4.1, 1st paragraph, last sentence, at the top of the right column (p. 6)
evidence.extracted: The review reports, second-hand from a study in ten healthy male volunteers, that clearance of S-ketamine was higher when it was given alone (26.3 mL/kg/min) than that of racemic ketamine (14.8 mL/kg/min), and that the clearance of the S-form inside the racemate (18.5 mL/kg/min) was lower than when it was given alone, which the authors read as R-ketamine inhibiting the elimination of S-ketamine; it also states that R-ketamine is not formed after intravenous S-ketamine in humans, so the two forms do not interconvert.

evidence.locator: Section 6 Pharmacodynamics and Clinical Use of Ketamine, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In its 2nd paragraph the review states that the two forms have similar pharmacokinetic profiles but different effects: some studies indicate the S-form may be about four times more potent than the R-form as an analgesic in humans while producing more auditory and visual disturbances, R-ketamine produces more agitation in surgical patients, emergence is faster after S-ketamine than after the R-form or the racemate, and the difference in analgesic efficiency is explained by S-ketamine's four times higher affinity for the NMDA receptor. The 1st paragraph gives effective concentrations for loss of consciousness of 241 ng/mL (SD 90) for the racemate and 111 (SD 30) for S-ketamine, taken from a textbook chapter.

The abstract writes the potency comparison as a postulate (the S-enantiomer has been postulated to be about four times more potent than the R-enantiomer and about two times more effective than the racemic mixture), while the Summary states the same comparison as fact; the review gives no primary measurement of its own for either figure.

risk_of_bias.note: Within-person, placebo-controlled and counterbalanced, but the blind did not hold (every participant recognised the (R)-ketamine condition and all had had a prior (S)-ketamine session), the ratings are partly self-reported and partly made by an unblinded psychiatrist, the method of counterbalancing is not described, and about 180 comparisons were made without correction (card sc_vollenweider_1997a, overall high).

inconsistency.note: One study for the psychopathological contrast; the direction was the same in all 10 participants. The three-person pharmacokinetic null result concerns a different outcome and is reported as a qualifier.

indirectness.note: The claim is about the two pure forms given in a laboratory, which is what was tested. The comparison with the racemic mixture is indirect, resting on a different sample in the companion paper, and the statement says so.

imprecision.note: Ten people in one laboratory; most outcomes are reported as percentage changes with significance levels and no intervals, and the smallest attainable two-sided p in these paired tests is 0.002.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from a single laboratory study; the study was supported in part by a pharmaceutical company, which the card records as a flag.

large_effect.note: Not applied: upgrades apply only to evidence that starts low (METHODS §6.3), although the difference was large and in the same direction in every participant.

grade.reasoning: A within-person, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced study starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: the blind did not hold for self-rated and observer-rated outcomes, and the reporting is selective and uncorrected. Imprecision −1: ten people in one laboratory, with no intervals or effect sizes printed. Low. The size of the contrast is nevertheless unusually clear for such a small study, because every participant scored higher under (S)-ketamine on both global scales. What the study cannot support is the further step to racemic ketamine as people encounter it, or the review's second-hand potency ratios, which the review itself calls a postulate.
